odor: Sharp, biting, reddish-brown gas — characteristic smell near traffic
environmentalPersistence: Low — atmospheric half-life hours to days; reacts with OH to form HNO₃

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Moderate — less than SO₂ at equivalent concentrations
morphologicalEffects.leafCurl: Moderate — mesophyll damage from nitrous/nitric acid formed internally
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Moderate — similar pattern to SO₂ but less severe; nitrous acid bleaches chlorophyll
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Moderate — interveinal necrosis similar to SO₂ but lighter
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: Mature leaves most sensitive; young leaves somewhat protected

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Moderate to strong — NO₂ generates reactive nitrogen species (peroxynitrite, •NO)

temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: Poor for necrotic tissue; partial stomatal recovery possible

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Green → pale interveinal → brown necrosis; similar to SO₂ but milder
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Interveinal necrosis pattern — similar to SO₂ but lighter; veins remain green
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Moderate — nitrate and nitrosylated protein signature
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: Partial — lighter scarring than SO₂; new growth recovers if source removed

synergies.synergyNote: NO₂ + SO₂ is the foundational acid rain precursor pair. NO₂ + ozone creates the photochemical smog cycle — NO₂ photolysis produces O atoms that form ozone, creating a self-reinforcing oxidative loop.

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Vehicle engines (primary source), power plants, industrial combustion — the reddish-brown haze over cities is largely NO₂
educationalContext.classification: Atmospheric pollutant / acid rain precursor / smog component
educationalContext.humanToxicity: High — respiratory damage; linked to asthma and cardiovascular disease; WHO standard: 40 µg/m³ annual mean
educationalContext.climateLink: NOₓ emissions (NO + NO₂) are central to tropospheric ozone formation and contribute to climate forcing
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Both — gas stoves and unvented heaters generate indoor NO₂; major outdoor traffic pollutant
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: The reddish-brown smog visible over cities on hot days — students can literally see NO₂. Gas stove NO₂ emissions are a current public health debate.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Urban smog, traffic pollution, gas stove indoor air quality, asthma epidemics in urban areas

sources: Wellburn AR (1990). Why are atmospheric oxides of nitrogen usually phytotoxic and not alternative fertilizers? New Phytologist, 115(3), 395–429.
Darrall NM (1989). The effect of air pollutants on physiological processes in plants. Plant, Cell & Environment, 12(1), 1–30.
Lovett GM, Tear TH (2008). Effects of nitrogen deposition on ecosystems. New Phytologist, 179(1), 1–2.
